title: Electromagnetic Induction and AC
lines: Electromagnetic induction is about one cause, a changing magnetic flux, and one result, an induced EMF. Faraday's law gives the size, Lenz's law gives the direction. Alternating current and transformers are applications of the same idea. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Magnetic flux

- Flux through a flat area S in a uniform field B: Φ = BS when B is perpendicular to the area; in general Φ = BS cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area. Unit: weber (1 Wb = 1 T·m²).
- Flux can change because B changes, because the area inside the field changes, or because the angle changes (rotation).
- Flux has a sign depending on which face the field enters. Turning a coil over by 180° in a field changes the flux by 2BS, not 0.
- The number of turns does not affect the flux through the coil; it multiplies the EMF.
> Example: A 0.5 m² loop sits in a 0.2 T field whose direction makes 60° with the normal to the loop. Find the flux.
## Faraday's law
- Induced EMF: E = nΔΦ/Δt, the rate of change of flux linkage. An EMF appears whenever the flux changes, even in an open circuit; a current flows only if the circuit is closed.
- On a Φ-t (or B-t) graph, the EMF is proportional to the gradient, not to the value. Where Φ is largest the EMF may be zero, and where Φ is zero the EMF may be largest.
- Charge passing through a circuit of total resistance R during a flux change: q = nΔΦ/R, independent of how fast the change happens.
> Example: A coil of 100 turns has its flux increased from 0.02 Wb to 0.08 Wb in 0.2 s. Find the average EMF. If the coil's circuit has total resistance 10 Ω, how much charge flows?
! Trap: large flux does not mean large EMF. Only a fast change of flux gives a large EMF.
## Lenz's law

- The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change of flux that causes it. If the flux increases, the induced field points against the original field; if it decreases, the induced field points the same way.
- Equivalent forms: "come close, get pushed; move away, get pulled"; a loop tends to shrink when the flux through it increases; induced currents oppose relative motion.
- Lenz's law is energy conservation: work must be done against the opposing force to produce the electrical energy.
> Example: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards one face of a coil. Which pole forms on that face, and which way does the current flow as seen from the magnet?
> The coil opposes the approach, so the near face becomes a north pole. By the right-hand grip rule, a north face seen from outside has anticlockwise current.
! Trap: "oppose" does not mean "prevent". The flux still changes, just less steeply than without the induced current.
## Motional EMF
- A straight conductor of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to B: E = BLv. If v makes angle θ with B, use the perpendicular component: E = BLv sin θ.

- Direction: right-hand rule. Field lines enter the palm, the thumb points along the velocity, the fingers give the current direction inside the rod. The end the current flows towards inside the rod is the positive terminal.

- With a closed circuit, current I = BLv/R flows and the rod feels a retarding force F = BIL = B²L²v/R. Pushing at constant speed needs a force equal to this, and the mechanical power Fv equals the electrical power EI.
- A rod falling or sliding under a constant driving force reaches a terminal speed when the magnetic force balances it.
- A rod of length L rotating about one end at angular speed ω: E = ½BωL² (use the average speed of the rod, ωL/2).
> Example: A 0.5 m rod slides at 4 m/s along rails in a 0.2 T field, in a circuit of total resistance 0.4 Ω. Find the EMF, the current, the retarding force and the power needed.
> Example: A horizontal rod of mass 0.01 kg and length 0.2 m falls along vertical smooth rails in a horizontal 0.5 T field; the circuit resistance is 0.1 Ω. Find the terminal speed.
## Self-induction

- A current changing in a coil changes its own flux, so the coil induces an EMF in itself that opposes the change in current: E = LΔI/Δt, where L is the inductance in henry (H). An iron core and more turns give a larger L.
- Switching on: a lamp in series with a large inductor lights up gradually.

- Switching off: a lamp connected in parallel with the coil may flash brighter before going out, but only if the coil's steady current was larger than the lamp's. The coil keeps its current flowing briefly through the lamp, in the reverse direction for the lamp.
> Example: The current in a 0.5 H coil falls from 2 A to 0 in 0.01 s. Find the average self-induced EMF.
> E = 0.5 × 2/0.01 = 100 V, much bigger than a typical supply voltage. This is why switches can spark.
## Alternating current

- A coil of n turns and area S rotating at ω in a uniform field B produces a sinusoidal EMF. Starting from the position where the coil plane is perpendicular to B (the neutral plane): e = E(m) sin ωt, with peak E(m) = nBSω.
- At the neutral plane, flux is greatest but the EMF is zero and the current changes direction (twice per turn). With the coil plane parallel to B, flux is zero and the EMF is greatest.
- Period T = 2π/ω, frequency f = 1/T. Mains in China: 220 V, 50 Hz, so the current reverses direction 100 times per second.

- The rms (effective) value is the steady DC value that gives the same heating in a resistor. For sine waves only: U(rms) = U(m)/√2 and I(rms) = I(m)/√2. Meter readings, ratings and power calculations use rms values.
- The peak of 220 V mains is 220√2 ≈ 311 V; capacitor and insulation ratings must survive the peak.
> Example: A coil with n = 100, B = 0.1 T, S = 0.02 m² rotates at ω = 100 rad/s. Find the peak and rms EMF. If it drives a 10 Ω resistor (ignore coil resistance), find the power.
! Trap: the average EMF over a quarter turn is not the rms value. Use E = nΔΦ/Δt for averages and charge, and rms for heat and power.
## Ideal transformers
- For an ideal transformer: U₁/U₂ = n₁/n₂, I₁/I₂ = n₂/n₁, and input power equals output power, P₁ = P₂.
- The output decides the input: if no load is connected the primary current is (ideally) zero; adding loads increases the primary current.
- A transformer does not work with steady DC, because the flux would not change. It does not change the frequency.
- Power transmission: line loss P(loss) = I²R(line). For a fixed power sent, raising the transmission voltage by a factor of k cuts the current by k and the loss by k².
> Example: A transformer steps 220 V mains down to 11 V for a 22 W lamp. Find the turns ratio and the primary current.
> n₁ : n₂ = 220 : 11 = 20 : 1. Input power = 22 W, so I₁ = 22/220 = 0.1 A (the lamp current is 22/11 = 2 A).
> Example: Power is sent along a line first at 10 kV, then at 100 kV, with the same power delivered. How does the line loss change?
> The current falls to 1/10, so the loss falls to 1/100.
! Trap: if you write the line loss as U²/R(line), U must be the voltage drop along the line itself, not the transmission voltage. Using the transmission voltage gives an absurdly large loss.
## Exam checklist
- Size from E = nΔΦ/Δt or BLv; direction from Lenz or the right-hand rule.
- Energy: work against magnetic forces becomes electrical energy and heat.
- AC: peak for insulation, rms for heating and meters, average for charge.
